content.text:
**I’d start with a separate pgvector table in the existing regional PlanetScale Postgres databases**, provided the extension is available on the actual clusters. It keeps vector search close to DataFn records and permissions, and makes updates and deletions easier to reason about. I would benchmark Cloudflare Vectorize before committing to that choice at scale: its published usage price is very low, but it adds a second index that must be kept in sync and its writes are asynchronous.

There are two repository details that matter before implementation. The existing `vector` DataFn resource is stored as JSONB in the generated Postgres mapping, so its `indices.vector` declaration is **not yet an ANN database index** ([schema definition](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/features.ts:347), [generated mapping](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/services/account/src/db/generated/datafn/datafn-schema.drizzle.ts:483)). Also, the fields currently marked `search` are for lexical SearchFn indexing: for example, `node` marks `label`, `text`, and `notes`, but not `mdText` or `bodySearch` ([schema](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/features.ts:230), [SearchFn mapping](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/search.provider.ts:71)). Decide explicitly which text to embed and how to chunk it; copying the lexical field list would omit some note content. The account service already has an *optional* OpenSearch SearchFn adapter, though I did not establish that an OpenSearch cluster is running in production ([adapter](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/services/account/src/datafn/search-provider.ts:19)).

| Choice | Strengths | Costs and constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **PlanetScale Postgres + pgvector** | One regional data system; SQL joins and permission filters; transactional vector updates alongside index records; fewer moving parts. Hyperdrive pooling has no separate usage charge on Workers Paid. PlanetScale also announced support for the `vectorscale` ANN extension. | Vector storage, ANN indexes, builds, and queries consume PlanetScale storage and compute alongside DataFn. Filtered ANN recall and latency need measurement with real user scopes. Hyperdrive improves connections but does not make a regional database globally local. Verify extension support on your **specific Postgres clusters**; PlanetScale’s widely advertised native vector indexes for MySQL are a different product. [PlanetScale extensions](https://planetscale.com/changelog/postgres-extension-vectorscale), [Hyperdrive pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/platform/pricing/), [pgvector filtering guidance](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector). |
| **Cloudflare Vectorize** | Managed index, Worker binding, namespaces and metadata filters, little index tuning, and low published usage pricing. | Separate projection and reconciliation jobs; upserts and deletes are asynchronous, so recently changed content may briefly appear stale. A query still needs a DataFn fetch and permission check before returning content. Current limits include 1,536 dimensions, 20 million vectors per index, 10 indexed metadata properties, and `topK` of 50 when returning metadata or values. [Pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/platform/pricing/), [limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/platform/limits/), [filtering](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/reference/metadata-filtering/), [write behavior](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/reference/client-api/). |
| **Existing OpenSearch, if deployed** | Can combine lexical and vector retrieval in one search service, with efficient filtered k-NN options. This is the strongest third option if you are already paying for and operating it. | Search-cluster capacity and operations; still a derived index with authorization and reconciliation work. I would not add an OpenSearch cluster solely for the present estimated volume without a benchmark. [OpenSearch filtering](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/vector-search/filter-search-knn/index/). |

For scale, **one million 1,024-dimensional float32 vectors contain about 4.1 GB of raw numbers** before Postgres row and index overhead. Under Cloudflare’s published formula, one million stored vectors and 100,000 searches in a month come to about **$11.78 before the Workers Paid included allocation**, or about **$11.27 after it**, excluding Worker execution and embedding generation. PlanetScale’s incremental bill cannot be inferred from raw bytes: instance size, replicas, storage, and query load determine it. Neither figure predicts latency; measure p50/p95 for user-filtered searches and record fetches in each serving region. [Vectorize formula](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/platform/pricing/), [PlanetScale pricing factors](https://planetscale.com/pricing).

For embeddings, **DigitalOcean has a standalone `POST /v1/embeddings` API**, with Qwen3 Embedding 0.6B shown in its request examples, up to 2,048 input strings per request, and published default limits of 250 requests/minute and 5,000/hour. Its model catalog also lists BGE-M3, among other open embedding models. DigitalOcean publishes **$0.04 per million tokens for Qwen3 Embedding 0.6B** and **$0.02 for BGE-M3** in its Knowledge Bases pricing section; confirm that the same rate and BGE-M3 access apply to your standalone API account before budgeting a full backfill. Serverless inference requires a positive prepaid balance. [API](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/api/reference/embeddings/), [models](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/models/), [pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/).

Cloudflare Workers AI currently lists **Qwen3 Embedding 0.6B and BGE-M3 at $0.012 per million input tokens** (rounded; their model pages show $0.0118). It includes 10,000 free neurons daily, then charges on Workers Paid; text embeddings have a published default limit of 3,000 requests/minute. Its asynchronous Batch API can handle a backfill, but I found no published batch discount. [Workers AI pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/pricing/), [limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/limits/), [batch API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/features/batch-api/).

An illustrative **one-million-record backfill at 500 embedded tokens per record** is 500 million input tokens: roughly **$20 at DigitalOcean’s published Qwen rate**, **$10 at its BGE-M3 rate**, or **$6 at Cloudflare’s listed rate**, before free allocation. Re-embedding changed records and embedding each search query incur the same token charge. These are inference estimates, separate from vector storage and search.

I checked `phidata` DynamoDB table metadata without reading user records. Its us-east-1 and ap-south-1 user tables report approximately **144,000 and 666,000 items**, respectively. Those approximate counts include record types that may never be embedded and say nothing about chunk count or token length, so they are not a production quote.

**The provider handoff is the main design risk in the proposed DigitalOcean-backfill/Cloudflare-ongoing split.** Use one versioned model and one document/query preprocessing contract. A shared model name does not prove that two providers return interchangeable vectors. Embed a representative sample through both, compare vectors and retrieval rankings, and use Cloudflare for ongoing writes only if that test passes. Otherwise keep the selected DigitalOcean model for ongoing generation, or re-embed the corpus with Cloudflare. Index each chunk with source ID, region, model version, content hash, and deletion state; re-read and authorize DataFn records before showing results. The older Memotron local generation path is currently disabled, so it is not an active migration pipeline ([local path](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/products/memotron/taco/taco.store.ts:12)).

My practical decision gate is a small, permission-aware pgvector prototype against the actual PlanetScale cluster, using the intended chunks and several real user-size scopes. Compare it with Vectorize on retrieval quality, p95 end-to-end latency, update visibility, and the **incremental PlanetScale bill**. No repository or cloud data was changed during this review.

content.text:
**Yes, the embedding API bill can be that small.** My $20 example was **1 million records × 500 tokens each × DigitalOcean’s published Qwen rate of $0.04 per million tokens**. Applying the same assumption to the approximately **809,721 items** reported by the two `phidata` DynamoDB tables gives **405 million tokens and about $16.19** for Qwen. At DigitalOcean’s published BGE-M3 rate, it would be about **$8.10**. Those rates appear in DigitalOcean’s Knowledge Bases pricing; I would confirm the standalone Embeddings API rate on the account before treating them as a quote. [DigitalOcean pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/), [Embeddings API](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/how-to/generate-vector-embeddings/).

The uncertainty is **how much text you actually embed**, not the arithmetic. DynamoDB’s count includes different item types, and a long note may produce several overlapping chunks while a title may contain only a few tokens. For roughly 810,000 eligible items:

| Average embedded tokens per item | Total tokens | DigitalOcean Qwen estimate |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100 | 81 million | $3.24 |
| 500 | 405 million | $16.20 |
| 2,000 | 1.62 billion | $64.80 |

These figures cover **embedding generation only**. Vector storage/search, re-embedding after edits or a model change, and query embeddings are separate. Embedding just titles would be cheap but would give poor recall for searches about the contents of notes.

**Quality can differ, but “closed” does not automatically mean “better.”** Hosting the *same* Qwen or BGE model on Cloudflare versus DigitalOcean should produce similar quality if the model version, query instructions, tokenization, truncation, and normalization match; I would test that before mixing vectors from the two hosts. Changing **models** can materially change which notes are retrieved, especially for vague queries, multilingual content, and long documents. Qwen3 and BGE-M3 are serious retrieval models, while a premium model such as Voyage 4 Large or OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` may justify its price on particular workloads. Published benchmarks are useful screening evidence, but they cannot establish which one works best on Memotron’s notes and search queries. [Qwen research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05176), [BGE-M3 research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03216), [MTEB benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316).

Using the **same 405-million-token assumption**, current listed generation prices look like this:

| Model/provider | Price per million tokens | Estimated backfill |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cloudflare Qwen3 or BGE-M3 | $0.012 | **$4.86**, before daily free allocation |
| DigitalOcean BGE-M3 | $0.02 | **$8.10** |
| OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` | $0.02 | **$8.10** |
| DigitalOcean Qwen3 0.6B | $0.04 | **$16.20** |
| Voyage 4 | $0.06 | **$24.30** list price |
| Voyage 4 Large | $0.12 | **$48.60** list price |
| OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` | $0.13 | **$52.65** |

[Cloudflare pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/pricing/), [DigitalOcean pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/), [OpenAI model pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/text-embedding-3-large), [Voyage pricing](https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/pricing). Voyage currently advertises an initial 200-million-token free allowance for its 4-series models, which could reduce a first backfill bill; the table shows list prices for an even comparison.

So the decision is unlikely to hinge on a **$10–$50 difference in the first embedding pass**. I’d evaluate Qwen3 0.6B, BGE-M3, and one premium retrieval model on a few hundred real Memotron queries with known relevant results, measuring recall among the top 10 and answer quality. The model that wins that test determines whether paying more is worthwhile. Also check vector dimensions: OpenAI’s large model defaults to 3,072 dimensions, exceeding Vectorize’s 1,536-dimension limit, although OpenAI supports shortening its output with a possible accuracy tradeoff. [OpenAI dimensions guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings), [Vectorize limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/vectorize/platform/limits/).

content.text:
I can start the evaluation with much of the access already in place. The `phidata` AWS profile works for **table metadata**, and Wrangler is logged into the 21n Cloudflare account. I found no Vectorize indexes there yet. I have **not** checked whether the AWS profile can read records or whether the Cloudflare login can create a test index. I also found no `doctl` or PlanetScale CLI installation; neither CLI is required if we have scoped API or database access.

What I need from you is:

1. **A representative search evaluation set.** Ideally 100–300 real queries, with the notes or records that *should* appear for each. Include short notes, long notes, vague queries, exact-name queries, and the languages users actually write in. This matters more than provider credentials: without expected results, I can compare speed and price but cannot tell you which model retrieves better answers.

2. **The content scope.** Which DataFn resources and fields should be embedded, whether old DynamoDB content and new Postgres content are both in scope, and whether private/shared records may be sent to DigitalOcean, Cloudflare, OpenAI, or Voyage for the evaluation. A small approved sample is enough for model selection. Please do not paste user content or API keys into chat.

3. **DigitalOcean model access.** A scoped **Inference Model Access Key**, supplied through the workspace’s secret mechanism or a local environment variable, with access to Qwen3 Embedding 0.6B and ideally BGE-M3. The account needs a positive serverless inference balance. We can test OpenAI or Voyage only if you want them in the comparison; each would need its own scoped API key.

4. **A disposable PlanetScale Postgres branch or staging database** in the same region and roughly the same compute class as the intended deployment. Database comparison needs permission there to enable the vector extension, create indexes, and load test vectors. A read-only connection to the current database would help measure record counts and tenant sizes, but cannot benchmark index creation and writes. I do not need production DDL access.

5. **Your decision targets:** expected search volume, acceptable p95 search latency, how soon edits/deletes must appear in results, regions or data-residency requirements, and a rough monthly budget. These determine whether Postgres’s simpler consistency is worth its incremental compute or Vectorize’s separate, asynchronous index is preferable.

With those, I’d measure retrieval quality (`recall@10` and ranking), query and indexing latency, filtered-search behavior across user permissions, update freshness, and projected monthly cost. I’d also test whether DigitalOcean and Cloudflare outputs for a nominally identical open model are compatible before recommending one for backfill and the other for ongoing writes.

**The minimum to begin is the approved content scope, a small set of expected search results, and DigitalOcean model access.** PlanetScale staging access is needed for the database decision. The existing AWS and Cloudflare sessions may cover the other provider access once their specific permissions are checked.
